The preceding subsections characterized dopamine as the biological implementation of a temporal-difference reward prediction error—a signed scalar whose burst-pause dynamics teach the striatum to optimize cumulative discounted reward. That characterization is not wrong, but it is incomplete. A growing body of experimental evidence, synthesized and extended by recent theoretical perspectives 1, 2, 3, reveals that at least some dopaminergic channels carry prediction errors over variables other than reward value: over the sensory identity of expected outcomes, over associative transitions between value-neutral states, over the degree of match between an intended and an executed action, and over the spatial trajectory taken toward a goal. Rather than constituting anomalies that strain the reward-RPE framework, these non-canonical signals are best understood as instances of a deeper engineering principle: the basal ganglia exploit a shared prediction-error architecture to solve multiple, partially distinct learning problems simultaneously, with different dopaminergic channels serving as the specialized teaching signals for each. The result is a system that is, in its functional logic, far closer to a general-purpose credit assignment engine than to a dedicated reward-tracking device. Experiments test whether dopamine-receptor activation requires spatially diffuse release. (Figure) 17. Spatially diffuse dopamine supports locomotion while point-to-point transmission supports learning. (Figure).

Perhaps the clearest and most extensively documented departure from pure reward-value coding concerns sensory and identity prediction errors. The conventional model-free RPE framework assigns dopamine the task of tracking a scalar cached value; it predicts that dopamine responses to outcome delivery should be sensitive to the amount and probability of reward but indifferent to the sensory identity of the reward so long as value is held constant. This prediction fails. Takahashi and colleagues recorded light-identified dopamine neurons in the VTA of rats while independently manipulating reward quantity (to drive value prediction errors) and reward flavor (to drive identity prediction errors at constant value). The same neurons that showed canonical burst responses to quantity increases also responded to unexpected flavor changes, and critically, the identity-driven changes in firing were not readily explainable as novelty or salience artifacts, nor did they track cached value–the 1st drop of a large reward, which should excite under value-RPE logic, instead did the opposite when its identity was unexpected, consistent with an identity-error signal rather than a value signal 4. Importantly, these identity- and value-driven responses were not confined to non-overlapping populations; most neurons that encoded value errors also encoded identity errors, suggesting that individual dopamine neurons carry multiplexed teaching signals over multiple outcome dimensions 4. Stalnaker and colleagues extended this finding by showing that the information about which sensory identity was mispredicted–not merely that a misprediction occurred–is encoded at the ensemble level across dopamine neurons in rats, and that analogous ensemble-level content specificity can be detected in the human midbrain BOLD signal, implicating dopamine in conveying content-rich rather than purely scalar teaching signals 5. In humans, Howard and Kahnt provided a mechanistic link downstream: identity prediction errors in the midbrain correlated with the updating of reward-identity expectations specifically in the orbitofrontal cortex, and not in areas that track value, suggesting that the OFC is a dedicated downstream recipient of identity-specific dopaminergic teaching signals 6. Further human work confirmed that these identity-error signals in the midbrain are independent of perceptual distance/similarity–they scale with the violation of identity expectations regardless of how perceptually similar the received and expected outcomes are 7. Recent circuit-level work has clarified which upstream structures supply the prediction of reward identity that must be subtracted: hippocampal lesions broadly impaired both value and identity error signaling by dopamine neurons, whereas OFC lesions produced a highly selective failure to extinguish identity-error responses despite relatively intact value-error signaling, indicating that OFC normally provides the learned identity expectation that is compared against received identity, while hippocampus is a more general memory supplier for the comparison 8. At the striatal level, identity-based dopamine signals have been shown to participate in sensory and perceptual decisions: striatal dopamine in the dorsal striatum integrates sensory prediction errors with reward prediction errors to guide perceptual choices, with dopamine release in both nucleus accumbens and dorsomedial striatum tracking errors in predicting value-neutral cues during latent learning as well as errors in predicting reward during reward-conditioning 9, 10. The unified implication is that the scope of what dopamine "predicts" is broader than reward magnitude: it can include the full featural content of expected outcomes, and its error signal updates both value and content representations in downstream targets. A 2025 mouse study examines prediction errors beyond reward (Figure). Striatal dopamine tracks sensory prediction errors during preconditioning (Figure).

The identity-error data already stretched the model-free RPE framework to its limits, because even a feature-augmented RPE model can, in principle, be reconciled with dopamine tracking the value of specific sensory events once those features are incorporated into the state representation. A more fundamental challenge comes from evidence that dopamine transients can drive learning about the associative transitions between entirely value-neutral stimuli–a form of learning that requires state prediction errors rather than reward prediction errors of any kind.

Sharpe and colleagues delivered a decisive causal test using a sensory preconditioning paradigm designed to isolate associative, value-free learning 11. The task has three phases. In preconditioning, rats experience repeated C→XC\rightarrow X pairings–two neutral cues presented in succession, with no reward–allowing an associative link between them to form. In conditioning, XX is separately paired with reward (the unconditioned stimulus, USUS). In a probe test, the rat is presented with CC alone: if it responds, it must be because it stored the C→XC\rightarrow X association during preconditioning and is now chaining it forward through XX to the remembered reward–a C→X→USC\rightarrow X\rightarrow US inference. This inference is model-based rather than model-free: CC was never directly paired with reward, so any cached value on CC must be zero (this was supported directly by a conditioned reinforcement probe in a parallel experiment, in which preconditioned cues–unlike directly conditioned cues–failed to support conditioned reinforcement, suggesting that they carry no cached value 12). Responding to CC in the probe test therefore reveals that the rat built and consulted an internal map of state transitions, not that it retrieved a stored value. A mouse study tests dopamine signals for sensory predictions (Figure). Striatal dopamine tracks value-based reward prediction errors during classical conditioning (Figure).

Having established the behavioral signature, Sharpe et al. then asked whether dopamine is the teaching signal that writes the C→XC\rightarrow X link. To test sufficiency, they incorporated a blocking design: cue AA was first trained to predict XX (A→XA\rightarrow X), then AA and CC were presented together before XX (AC→XAC\rightarrow X). Because AA already predicts XX, there is no prediction error at the C→XC\rightarrow X transition, and standard blocking was confirmed–CC-learning was suppressed. The key manipulation then delivered a brief optogenetic burst to VTA dopamine neurons precisely at the moment of the AC→XAC\rightarrow X transition on blocked trials, artificially reinstating a prediction error where none existed. This unblocked CC-learning: rats now responded robustly to CC in the probe test, despite CC being entirely redundant throughout training 11. To test necessity, halorhodopsin was used to suppress dopamine neurons at the B→YB\rightarrow Y transition during a standard sensory preconditioning task; this selectively attenuated probe-test responding to BB while leaving a control cue unaffected. Together, these findings provide strong causal evidence that transient VTA dopamine activity is sufficient, and likely necessary, for acquisition of reward-free cue-cue associations that later support model-based behavior.

A follow-up study closed the loop on the model-free alternative: using three controlled experiments, Sharpe and colleagues showed that optogenetic dopamine activation in the identical sensory-preconditioning setting enhanced associative (model-based) representations without endowing antecedent cues with cached value, as confirmed by conditioned reinforcement probes 13. The dopamine transient functioned as an associative credit assignment signal rather than a value signal, contradicting the assumption that dopamine transients are restricted to model-free reinforcement learning. The theoretical framework that best accommodates these findings treats dopamine as a generalized prediction error signal 14: rather than being restricted to reward predictions, dopaminergic error signals may span the full spectrum of prediction-error-driven learning–from cached reward-value updating at one end to model-based state-transition learning at the other–retaining all the successes of the RPE hypothesis while explaining why dopamine participates in sensory preconditioning and identity unblocking, paradigms that are entirely opaque to pure model-free theories. Kahnt and Schoenbaum’s 2025 review synthesizes this evidence alongside related human findings to conclude that the hypothesis of a strictly value-based dopaminergic teaching signal should be replaced by a framework in which dopamine tracks errors over a richer representational space that includes stimulus identity, associative structure, and contextual transitions 2.

Adding to this story, a distinct functional dimension emerges from the tail of the striatum, which receives dopaminergic input from neurons in the lateral SNc and substantia nigra pars lateralis (SNl) that respond prominently to movement rather than reward. Greenstreet and colleagues used an auditory discrimination task in mice to ask whether the movement-related dopamine activity in this region encodes the theoretical action prediction error (APE)–defined as the discrepancy between the action that was taken and the action that was predicted given the animal’s past actions (regardless of value) 15. The prediction term here is not a value forecast but an action prior: the degree to which a particular movement was expected given the current sensory context and the animal’s history of state-action associations. On repeated trials, well-practiced actions become strongly predicted by their antecedent sensory states; novel or inconsistent actions remain poorly predicted. The APE is therefore large when the executed action deviates from this internally maintained action prior, and small or zero when the animal does exactly what its prior history leads it to expect of itself. Fiber photometry confirmed that tail-of-striatum dopamine signals behave accordingly: they increased when the executed action deviated from prediction and decreased when actions were well-predicted, independently of reward. Causal manipulations using optogenetic activation and suppression confirmed that this APE signal serves as a value-free teaching signal: stimulation of tail-of-striatum dopamine neurons drove the reinforcement of repeated state-action associations without endowing those actions with reward value, and suppression impaired the learning of stable sound-action mappings 15. Computational modeling showed that APE and RPE signals are complementary rather than redundant: APE alone cannot support reward-guided learning (because it carries no information about outcome value), but when paired with RPE circuitry it consolidates stable sensorimotor associations in a value-free manner–essentially locking in action mappings that RPE has already established as broadly correct. This constitutes a second dopaminergic learning system operating in parallel with the canonical mesolimbic reward-RPE system, specialized for the formation of habits defined by repetition consistency rather than by reward history 15. The empirical separation between APE and RPE dopaminergic populations is anatomically precise: RPE is predominantly encoded in VTA and medial SNc projecting to ventral and dorsomedial striatum, while APE resides in lateral SNc and SNl projecting to posterior and tail striatum. In this sense the spatial multiplexing of teaching signals across striatal territories (already emphasized in the distributional and multi-timescale discussion above) extends to include a qualitative division: the posterior striatal axis carries a learning signal defined over the action dimension, not the value dimension. Consistent with this, Brown and colleagues recently showed that cue-evoked dopamine release in the striatum encodes bidirectional trajectory errors–the discrepancy between an animal’s ongoing speed and direction relative to an optimal trajectory toward a goal–entirely independently from simultaneous dopamine signals reflecting learned cue value, with the two signals separable in timing and regional prevalence across the striatum 16. Computational analysis revealed that a standard RPE algorithm supplied with mixed sensorimotor inputs can simultaneously reproduce both cue-value and trajectory-error coding, suggesting that the error-signal infrastructure is shared but the inputs that drive it differ across dopamine subpopulations, yielding functionally distinct teaching signals from a common algorithmic substrate. A 2025 mouse study tests the tail of the striatum in action learning (Figure). A 2025 mouse study measures dopamine signals consistent with action prediction errors (Figure). The study tests whether tail-striatal dopamine reinforces state–action associations (Figure).

Taken together, the evidence reviewed in this section converges on a view that is difficult to reconcile with any narrow interpretation of dopamine as a dedicated reward-value tracker. Recent work by Gershman and colleagues 1 frames three major empirical challenges to the classical RPE theory–ramping dopamine signals during approach to reward, responsivity to sensory and motor features, and influence on action selection–and argue that each can be addressed by suitably generalizing the prediction-error concept rather than abandoning it. In their account, ramps can arise from TD-like prediction errors under realistic assumptions about convex value estimates and state uncertainty; sensory and identity-related responses can be understood either through model-based updating of internal transition/reward models or through generalized, vector-valued prediction errors over non-reward features; and action-related signals may reflect action prediction errors or related control signals embedded within RL architectures for choice, vigor, and average reward. However, Gershman et al. also emphasize that this generalized synthesis is still incomplete: a full theory of dopamine likely must incorporate additional mechanisms related to salience, causal inference, precision, and adaptive learning-rate control. Their proposed direction is therefore not a rejection of prediction-error theory, but an expansion from scalar reward-RPE toward richer, structured prediction-error signals that can update generalized value functions and, potentially, components of a world model 1. Imaging identifies localized dopamine release hotspots during ongoing behavior (Figure).

Overall, recent work suggests that the basal ganglia do not implement one optimizer tracking one objective through one teaching signal. Instead, they implement a portfolio of prediction-error channels, anatomically distinguished at the level of projection-defined dopamine subpopulations and their striatal targets, each specialized for a different learning problem: value learning in mesolimbic circuits, identity and associative structure learning in circuits coupling OFC and dorsomedial striatum to midbrain, sensorimotor habit consolidation in lateral SNc-to-posterior striatum channels, and trajectory optimization in SNl-to-tail-striatum channels. What unifies these channels is not a shared objective but a shared computational motif: each computes a prediction error relative to some expected state of the world (defined over different state spaces and different prediction horizons), broadcasts that error via dopaminergic release, and uses it to update the synaptic weights of the circuits that generated the prediction. This implies that dopamine is best understood not as a neurotransmitter synonymous with reward, but as a general-purpose credit assignment signal–one whose reward-value channel is the best-characterized instance of a much larger family of error signals through which the basal ganglia continuously update a distributed, structured model of the agent’s world.
